# Introduction

This blog is built with [Quarto](https://quarto.org/). A Quarto document keeps text, code, and the resulting figures and tables together in a `.qmd` file. For a geography project, that can mean a map alongside the code that produced it and a paragraph explaining the pattern.

When an analysis changes, rerunning the code and rendering the document updates the outputs. Reproducing the result also requires the data and a compatible software environment.

This post covers installation, the structure of a `.qmd` file, and a few examples using spatial data. Most examples use R. The appendix adds Python through `reticulate`, followed by an interactive plot in Observable JS.

## Output formats

The same source can be rendered as HTML, PDF, Word, or Revealjs slides. You can reuse the analysis code, though layouts and interactive elements may need adjustments for each format.

::: callout-tip
[To try another output format, change `format: html` to `format: docx` or `format: pdf`](#sec-output-options), then render again. The interactive examples in this post are designed for HTML; PDF and Word may need static alternatives.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## PDF output with TinyTeX

The default `pdf` format uses LaTeX. If you do not already have a TeX distribution, [Quarto recommends TinyTeX](https://quarto.org/docs/output-formats/pdf-basics.html). Install it from a terminal:

```bash

quarto install tinytex

```

:::

## Equations

Quarto supports [LaTeX math syntax](#latex-math-mode). For example, Moran's I can be written as:

$$I = \frac{n}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}w_{ij}} \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}w_{ij}(z_i-\bar{z})(z_j-\bar{z})}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(z_i-\bar{z})^2}$$

## An interactive map

HTML is a useful starting point for spatial work because readers can explore a map directly. In the example below, zoom in or click on a country to inspect its attributes.

```{r}
#| label: interactive-map
#| fig-cap: "Global Life Expectancy Map"

# Load necessary spatial libraries
library(sf)
library(tmap)

# Set tmap mode to interactive 'view' for HTML output
tmap_mode("view")

# Load built-in World dataset for demonstration
data(World)

# Create an interactive map showing life expectancy
tm_shape(World) +
  tm_polygons("life_exp", 
              palette = "YlGnBu", 
              title = "Life Expectancy",
              id = "name",
              popup.vars = c("pop_est", "gdp_cap_est"))

```



# Installing Quarto

The examples below assume that [R](https://www.r-project.org/){target="_blank"} and [RStudio](https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/){target="_blank"} are already installed.

## Windows


On Windows, you can install Quarto with the Windows Package Manager, `winget`.

### Open a terminal

Use either of these:

1. **Inside RStudio:** Click the **Terminal** tab (located right next to the **Console** tab) and paste the commands there.
2. **Windows Terminal:** Press **`Win + R`**, type `wt` (or `powershell`), and hit Enter to open a standalone terminal window.

### Installation Script (PowerShell)

Paste the block below into the terminal. Lines beginning with `#` are comments; uncomment the R or RStudio commands if you need those too.


```powershell

# If your machine doesn't have R and its components...
# Un-comment the lines below (remove the '#') to install them
# winget install -e --id RProject.R
# winget install -e --id RProject.Rtools
# winget install -e --id Posit.RStudio

# install Quarto
winget install -e --id Posit.Quarto

```


::: {.callout-note}
A university-managed computer may require IT approval for installation. If `winget` is unavailable, use the [Quarto installer](https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/) or check with your IT team.
:::

## macOS

With Homebrew installed, run:

```zsh
# Install Quarto
brew install --cask quarto

# Optional: Install R & RStudio
# brew install --cask r
# brew install --cask rstudio

```

::: {.callout-note}
If you need Homebrew, start at [brew.sh](https://brew.sh/){target="_blank"}. Installation on a university-managed Mac may require help from IT.
:::


## Linux Variants

If Linux is your primary OS, I’m sure you already know how to install it without my help.


# Basic Usage


## What goes into a `.qmd` file?

A Quarto document has three main parts. Click the `</> Code` button at the top right of this page to see them in the source.

1. **YAML header:** Settings such as the title, author, and output format.
2. **Markdown text:** The written content, including headings, links, and equations.
3. **Code chunks:** Code that loads data, runs an analysis, or creates a figure.


### YAML Header

```yaml
---
title: "A Glimpse into Quarto"
subtitle: "Getting started with R, Python, and spatial data"
author: "Yonghun Suh"
date: "Mar. 9, 2026"
categories: [Code]
image: https://rstudio.github.io/cheatsheets/html/images/quarto-illustration.png
format: 
  html:
    number_sections: true
    code-copy: true
    code-fold: show
    code-tools: true
    code-overflow: scroll
    code-link: true
    number-sections: true
    toc: true
    toc_depth: 3
    lightbox: true
# Excute options
execute:
  warning: false
  message: false
---
```

### Document body

#### Markdown text {- #sec-markdown-text}

Write the body of the document in Markdown. Headings, lists, links, and other formatting use plain-text notation, as in the examples below.

##### Basic Markdown syntax {-}

For example:

```md
* **Bold text** for emphasis.
* *Italic text* for variables or terms.
* `Inline code` for package names like `sf` or `terra`.

1. Ordered list for methodologies.
2. Second step in the workflow.

```

##### LaTeX math {- #latex-math-mode}

Use [LaTeX notation](https://www.overleaf.com/learn/latex/Mathematical_expressions){target="_blank"} to write equations. Single dollar signs mark inline math; double dollar signs put an equation on its own line.

```md
* **Inline math:** Use single dollar signs. For example, the distance threshold is $d_{ij} \le 50$.

```

* **Inline math:** Use single dollar signs. For example, the distance threshold is $d_{ij} \le 50$.


* **Display math:** Use double dollar signs for standalone equations. Here is the formula for a basic spatial lag model:

```md
$$
y = \rho W y + X \beta + \varepsilon
$$

```

$$
y = \rho W y + X \beta + \varepsilon
$$


##### Links and media {-}

Links and images use similar syntax. This example links to the Quarto documentation and embeds a local video of the Aral Sea.

```md
* Inserting a web link
    * [Official Quarto Documentation](https://quarto.org/)

* Inserting a local image with a caption
![\nTemporal Changes of Our Study Area: Aral Sea](data/Aral_Landsat.mp4)

```

##### Wider figures and margin notes {-}

A detailed map may need more width than the main text column. Quarto's article layout options let you place content across the page or in a margin. Wrap the content in a fenced div (`:::`) with the appropriate class:

```md
::: {.column-page}
![This figure extends beyond the text column.](https://rstudio.github.io/cheatsheets/html/images/quarto-illustration.png)
:::
```

::: {.column-page}
![This figure extends beyond the text column.](https://rstudio.github.io/cheatsheets/html/images/quarto-illustration.png)
:::



```md
::: {.column-margin}
This note appears in the right margin.
:::

```

::: {.column-margin}
This note appears in the right margin.
:::

> For a figure produced by a code chunk, use `#| column: page` to extend it across the page or `#| column: screen` for the full browser width. See the [article layout documentation](https://quarto.org/docs/authoring/article-layout.html){target="_blank"} for other options.


```{r}
#| label: interactive-map-layout
#| fig-cap: "Global Life Expectancy Map"
#| column: page

# Load necessary spatial libraries
library(sf)
library(tmap)

# Set tmap mode to interactive 'view' for HTML output
tmap_mode("view")

# Load built-in World dataset for demonstration
data(World)

# Create an interactive map showing life expectancy
tm_shape(World) +
  tm_polygons("life_exp", 
              palette = "YlGnBu", 
              title = "Life Expectancy",
              id = "name",
              popup.vars = c("pop_est", "gdp_cap_est"))

```


##### Callouts and footnotes {-}

Use a footnote for a short aside or reference, and a callout for a note you want readers to notice.

```md
Here is a statement that needs a reference.^[This will automatically generate a numbered footnote at the bottom of the page.]

```

Here is a statement that needs a reference.^[This will automatically generate a numbered footnote at the bottom of the page.]

```md
::: {.callout-important}
## Attention
Always check your Coordinate Reference System (CRS) before performing spatial joins!
:::

```

::: {.callout-important}
## Attention
Always check your Coordinate Reference System (CRS) before performing spatial joins!
:::

#### Code chunks {- #sec-code-chunks}

Executable code goes in a fenced block with a language name in braces, such as `{r}` or `{python}`. When the document is rendered, the chunk can run and include its output.

##### Chunk options {-}

Put chunk options on lines beginning with `#|` at the top of the block. A few useful ones are listed below; the [execution options documentation](https://quarto.org/docs/computations/execution-options.html) has more.

| Option | Value | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `#| echo:` | `true` / `false` | Shows or hides the source code in the output. |
| `#| eval:` | `true` / `false` | Determines whether to run the code. Useful for showing syntax only. |
| `#| warning:` | `true` / `false` | Shows warnings when `true`; hides them when `false`. |
| `#| cache:` | `true` / `false` | Reuses cached computation results; useful for slow chunks. |

##### R and Python {-}

R documents use Knitr, while Python documents commonly use Jupyter. To use both languages in a Knitr document, `reticulate` lets you exchange objects between R and Python. The appendix shows this with a regression example and a clustering example.

---

##### Example: plotting growth rates {-}


::: callout-tip
## Reading the plot {-}

The curves below illustrate common growth rates. Here, $n$ is input size and $N$ is a schematic operation count. They show how computational cost can grow with input size; they are not measured runtimes.

[Learn more](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_complexity){target="_blank"}
:::

```{r, warning=FALSE}
#| fig-cap: "Comparison of computational growth rates"
#| fig-subcap: "Schematic growth rates, not measured runtimes."
#| fig-alt: "Curves comparing constant, logarithmic, linear, and faster growth rates"

library(data.table)
library(ggplot2)

# Seq `n` gen
n <- seq(0, 100, by = 0.01)  # need to make the increment small in order to avoid `Inf`s

# data.table
df <- data.table(
                  n = n,
                  `O(1)` = 1,
                  `O(log n)` = log2(n),
                  `O(n)` = n,
                  `O(n log n)` = n * log2(n),
                  `O(n^2)` = n^2,
                  `O(2^n)` = 2^n,
                  `O(n!)` = factorial(n)
                )

df_long <- data.table::melt(df, id.vars = "n", variable.name = "Complexity", value.name = "Time")

ggplot(df_long, aes(x = n, y = Time, color = Complexity)) +
      geom_line(size = 1.2) +
            ylim(1, 100) +
            xlim(1, 100)+
      labs(
            #title = "Compirison of Computational Complexity",
            x = "Input Size (n)",
            y = "Number of Operations (N)",
            color = "Complexity"
          ) +
      theme_minimal() +
      theme(
            plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"),
            legend.title = element_text(size = 12),
            legend.text = element_text(size = 10)
      )

```




# Appendix

## Using other languages in Quarto

The snippets below illustrate code-block syntax for several languages. Running them requires the appropriate runtime and execution setup. The worked R and Python examples that follow use Knitr with `reticulate`.

1. `R`
```{{r}}
print_a <- function(a) {
  a <- 1 
  print(paste("Inside function:", a))
}
```


2. `Python`

```{{python}}

def print_a(a):

    a = 1
    print(f"Inside function: {a}")

```

3. `Julia`

```{{julia}}

function print_a(a)
    println("Inside function: $a")
end

```

4. `Fortran`

```{{fortran}}

subroutine printA(A)
    implicit none
    
    integer, intent(in) :: A
    
    print*, "The value is:", A    
    
end subroutine printA


```

### R and Python with reticulate

The first chunk shows which Python executable `reticulate` is using. In this blog's build, Python and its packages are managed by Pixi.


```{r}
library(reticulate)

# The One-pass renderer provisions Pixi's Python and packages from
# ci-packages. No new Conda environment or machine-specific path is needed.

sys <- import("sys")

sys$executable

```



#### OLS and maximum likelihood {-}

In linear regression, we model the relationship between a dependent variable and independent variables as:

$$y = X\beta + \epsilon$$

For $N$ observations and $K$ coefficients, the dimensions are:

* $y \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 1}$: Dependent variable vector. 
* $X \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times K}$: Design matrix (including a column of 1s for the intercept). 
* $\beta \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times 1}$: Parameter (coefficient) vector. 
* $\epsilon \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 1}$: Error vector.

::: {.panel-tabset}

#### OLS Perspective: Minimizing the SSR

The Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) method seeks to find $\beta$ that minimizes the Sum of Squared Residuals ($SSR$):

$$SSR(\beta) = \epsilon^T \epsilon = (y - X\beta)^T (y - X\beta)$$

##### Expanding the objective {-}

Expand the expression as follows.

1. Distribution of Transpose

Using the rules $(A - B)^T = A^T - B^T$ and $(AB)^T = B^T A^T$:

$$(y - X\beta)^T = y^T - (X\beta)^T = y^T - \beta^T X^T$$

2. Expanding the product

Now we multiply $(y^T - \beta^T X^T)$ by $(y - X\beta)$:

$$SSR(\beta) = y^T y - y^T X \beta - \beta^T X^T y + \beta^T X^T X \beta$$

3. The Scalar Property (Merging Terms)

Note that $y^T X \beta$ is a scalar ($1 \times 1$). Any scalar is equal to its own transpose ($a = a^T$):

$$(y^T X \beta)^T = \beta^T X^T (y^T)^T = \beta^T X^T y$$

Since they are identical values, we can combine the middle terms:

$$SSR(\beta) = y^T y - 2\beta^T X^T y + \beta^T X^T X \beta$$

##### The normal equation {-}

Taking the partial derivative with respect to $\beta$:

$$\frac{\partial SSR}{\partial \beta} = -2X^T y + 2X^T X \beta = 0$$

If $X$ has full column rank, solving for $\beta$ gives:

$$\hat{\beta}_{OLS} = (X^T X)^{-1} X^T y$$

#### MLE Perspective: Maximum Likelihood


For this example, assume independent Gaussian errors with constant variance: $\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 I)$. The log-likelihood is:

$$\mathcal{L}(\beta, \sigma^2) = -\frac{N}{2}\ln(2\pi\sigma^2) - \frac{1}{2\sigma^2} \sum_{i=1}^{N} (y_i - X_i\beta)^2$$

For a fixed positive $\sigma^2$, maximizing this expression with respect to $\beta$ is equivalent to minimizing $SSR$. OLS and maximum likelihood therefore give the same regression coefficients under this model.

:::

#### Fitting the model across R and Python

The `meuse` soil dataset from the `sp` package provides a small example. Here, zinc concentration ($y$) is modeled using copper concentration ($x$).

##### Prepare the data in R

```{r}
#| label: data-preparation
library(sp)
library(reticulate)

# Load Meuse dataset
data(meuse)

# Prepare Design Matrix X (adding an intercept column of 1s) and Target Vector y
y_vec <- as.matrix(meuse$zinc)
x_mat <- as.matrix(cbind(1, meuse$copper))

cat("Number of observations (N):", nrow(x_mat), "\n")

```

##### Fit the model in Python

Python accesses the R objects through `r.x_mat` and `r.y_vec`. NumPy solves the OLS normal equations, and SciPy estimates the parameters by numerical optimization.

```{python}
#| label: python-ols-mle
import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import minimize

# 1. Retrieve variables from R environment
X = r.x_mat
y = r.y_vec
N = X.shape[0]

# =========================================================
# Step 1: Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) via Linear Algebra
# =========================================================
def compute_ols(X_matrix: np.ndarray, y_vector: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """
    Compute OLS coefficients using the Normal Equation.

    Args:
        X_matrix (np.ndarray): Design matrix.
        y_vector (np.ndarray): Target vector.

    Returns:
        np.ndarray: Beta coefficients.
    """
    xtx = X_matrix.T @ X_matrix
    xty = X_matrix.T @ y_vector
    return np.linalg.solve(xtx, xty)

beta_ols = compute_ols(X, y)

print("--- 1. OLS Results (NumPy Linear Algebra) ---")
print(f"Intercept: {beta_ols[0][0]:.4f}")
print(f"Slope (Copper): {beta_ols[1][0]:.4f}\n")

# =========================================================
# Step 2: Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) via Optimization
# =========================================================
def negative_log_likelihood(params: np.ndarray) -> float:
    """
    Calculate the Negative Log-Likelihood for a Gaussian regression model.

    Args:
        params (np.ndarray): Array containing [intercept, slope, variance].

    Returns:
        float: The NLL value to be minimized.
    """
    beta = params[0:2].reshape(-1, 1)
    variance = params[2]

    # Mathematical constraint: Variance must be strictly positive
    if variance <= 0:
        return np.inf

    # Calculate Sum of Squared Residuals (SSR)
    residuals = y - (X @ beta)
    ssr = np.sum(residuals ** 2)

    # Calculate NLL formula
    nll = (N / 2) * np.log(2 * np.pi * variance) + (ssr / (2 * variance))
    return float(nll)

# Initial guess for the optimizer: [intercept=0, slope=0, variance=10]
initial_guess = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 10.0])

# Run L-BFGS-B optimization algorithm to find the MLE parameters
mle_result = minimize(negative_log_likelihood, initial_guess, method='L-BFGS-B')

beta_mle = mle_result.x[0:2]
variance_mle = mle_result.x[2]

print("--- 2. MLE Results (SciPy Optimization) ---")
print(f"Intercept: {beta_mle[0]:.4f}")
print(f"Slope (Copper): {beta_mle[1]:.4f}")
print(f"Estimated Variance: {variance_mle:.4f}\n")

# =========================================================
# Step 3: Verify Mathematical Equivalence
# =========================================================
diff = np.abs(beta_ols.flatten() - beta_mle)
print("--- 3. Equivalence Check (Difference |OLS - MLE|) ---")
print(f"Difference in Intercept: {diff[0]:.2e}")
print(f"Difference in Slope: {diff[1]:.2e}")

```

##### Compare with R's `lm()`

Fit the same model with `lm()` and compare the coefficients:

```{r}
#| label: r-verification
# Fit OLS using R's built-in linear model function
r_lm <- lm(zinc ~ copper, data = meuse)

cat("--- R's lm() Coefficients ---\n")
print(coef(r_lm))

```

::: {.callout-note}
## Small differences in the estimates

The two methods target the same regression coefficients here, but the implementations use different numerical procedures. NumPy solves a linear system; SciPy iterates until a stopping condition is met. If the estimates differ, check `mle_result.success`, the optimizer's tolerances, and numerical scaling before interpreting the difference. See [SciPy's L-BFGS-B documentation](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/optimize.minimize-lbfgsb.html) for the stopping criteria.

:::

#### Clustering points: R $\rightarrow$ Python $\rightarrow$ R {-}

This example sends the `quakes` data frame from R to Python, runs DBSCAN with `scikit-learn`, and brings the cluster labels back to R for plotting. It shows how a data frame and an array move between the two languages.

```{r}
#| label: load-spatial-points
# Load built-in Fiji earthquakes dataset
data(quakes)

# Select spatial coordinates and magnitude
spatial_df <- quakes[, c("lat", "long", "mag")]
head(spatial_df, 3)

```

```{python}
#| label: python-clustering
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.cluster import DBSCAN

def perform_spatial_clustering(df: pd.DataFrame, eps: float = 2.0, min_samples: int = 15) -> np.ndarray:
    """
    Apply DBSCAN clustering algorithm to spatial coordinates.

    Args:
        df (pd.DataFrame): DataFrame containing 'lat' and 'long' columns.
        eps (float): The maximum distance between two samples for one to be considered
                     as in the neighborhood of the other.
        min_samples (int): The number of samples in a neighborhood for a point
                           to be considered as a core point.

    Returns:
        np.ndarray: Array of cluster labels (-1 indicates noise).
    """
    # Extract coordinates as a NumPy array
    coords = df[['lat', 'long']].values

    # Initialize and fit DBSCAN
    clustering_model = DBSCAN(eps=eps, min_samples=min_samples)
    labels = clustering_model.fit_predict(coords)

    return labels

# r.spatial_df is automatically converted to a Pandas DataFrame
cluster_labels = perform_spatial_clustering(r.spatial_df)

```

```{r}
#| label: plot-clusters
library(ggplot2)

# Bind the Python-generated labels back to the R dataframe
spatial_df$cluster <- as.factor(py$cluster_labels)

# Plot the cluster labels in R
ggplot(spatial_df, aes(x = long, y = lat, color = cluster, size = mag)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_color_viridis_d(option = "plasma", name = "Cluster\n(-1 = Noise)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Spatial Clustering of Fiji Earthquakes",
    subtitle = "DBSCAN computed in Python, Plotted in R",
    x = "Longitude",
    y = "Latitude"
  )

```

The [DBSCAN default](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.cluster.DBSCAN.html) is Euclidean distance. In this example, `eps = 2` is in coordinate degrees because the inputs are latitude and longitude. For a geographic distance threshold, use a suitable projection or a spherical distance metric.

### Observable JS in the browser

Observable JS can add controls and plots to an HTML document. Here, R creates sample data when the code is executed, and [`ojs_define()`](https://quarto.org/docs/interactive/ojs/data-sources.html) makes it available to the OJS chunk. The station selector then filters the data in the browser without rerunning R.

#### Create the data in R {-}

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(data.table)

# 1. Generate sample environmental data (e.g., temperature across stations)
set.seed(42)
dt_env <- data.table(
  station = rep(c("Station_A", "Station_B", "Station_C"), each = 50),
  day = rep(1:50, 3),
  temperature = c(rnorm(50, 15, 2), rnorm(50, 18, 3), rnorm(50, 12, 1.5))
)

# 2. Export the data to the Observable JS environment
ojs_define(env_data = dt_env)

```

#### Plot it with Observable JS {-}

Choose a station from the dropdown to update the plot.

```{ojs}
//| echo: true
//| code-fold: false

// 1. Transpose the data (R data frames become column-major JSON arrays, OJS needs row-major)
data = transpose(env_data)

// 2. Create a reactive dropdown input
viewof selected_station = Inputs.select(
  ["Station_A", "Station_B", "Station_C"], 
  {label: "Select Station:"}
)

// 3. Filter data based on user selection
filtered_data = data.filter(d => d.station === selected_station)

// 4. Render the plot using Observable Plot
Plot.plot({
  y: {
    grid: true,
    label: "Temperature (°C)"
  },
  x: {
    label: "Day of Observation"
  },
  marks: [
    Plot.line(filtered_data, {x: "day", y: "temperature", stroke: "steelblue", strokeWidth: 2}),
    Plot.dot(filtered_data, {x: "day", y: "temperature", fill: "black"})
  ]
})

```

### System information

The last chunk prints basic system information from the machine that executes the code.

```{r}
if (Sys.info()[[1]]=="Windows") {

    # For my Windows Environment
    system("systeminfo",intern = T)


    } else{

    system("lscpu; free -h",intern = T)



}
```
